verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and none fails level 1a or 1b. Three fixable level 2 points remain: standards-compat-1 (single-row locking and fewer volatile evaluations in existing UNION queries), maintenance-fit-2 (the HashAgg gate uses the SetOp estimator and changes existing DISTINCT plans), and maintenance-fit-3 (no planning-time numbers). The thread has one message and no review, so confidence is low.

brief.title: Parallel partial de-duplication and implicit LIMIT 1 for UNION
brief.problem: For low-cardinality inputs, a parallel hash-based UNION does all de-duplication in one HashAggregate above Gather, so the leader reads every row from every child. A set-operation child whose output is one constant tuple still scans all matching rows. DISTINCT already handles both cases, so UNION queries are slower than the equivalent DISTINCT over UNION ALL.
brief.proposed_design: Patch 1 moves the shared DISTINCT/setop path construction into planner.c helpers and adds a hash_mem check for the partial DISTINCT hash path when the group estimate is unreliable. Patch 2 adds a worker-local HashAggregate below Gather for UNION through a new UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP stage, with the final HashAggregate in the leader. Patch 3 adds LIMIT 1 to constant children of non-ALL UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT, including partial paths.
user_visible_surface: New upper relation stage UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP, passed to create_upper_paths_hook with a NULL input relation; it may be called more than once per query.
New selfuncs C API: estimate_num_groups_unreliable() and the SELFLAG_USED_MULTIVAR_CLAMP flag.
New plan shapes in EXPLAIN: partial HashAggregate under Gather for UNION, and Limit 1 on constant set-operation children.
Fewer evaluations of volatile quals, FROM items or CTEs in constant set-operation children, and locking clauses in a non-pullable subquery or CTE may lock only the first row.
author_claims: Low-cardinality UNION of 2 to 4 tables of 1M rows runs about 2.6 to 2.8 times faster.
A constant branch plus a varying branch runs about 4 times faster in parallel and 1.7 times faster serially.
Near-unique keys, UNION ALL, DISTINCT, INTERSECT, EXCEPT and grouped-child queries show no change within noise.
The early-stopping behavior matches existing SELECT DISTINCT LIMIT 1 behavior, so it has precedent.
make check, make check-world and a cassert Meson build pass.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible; nobody has replied. The author asks whether early stopping with locking clauses is acceptable for set operations, or whether children with rowMarks should be excluded.
unclear: The benchmarks come from one laptop under WSL2 with 4 runs each; the material gives no planning-time cost for the extra paths.
The author does not say why EstimateSetOpHashTableSpace() fits HashAgg, beyond one 200k-row case that chose the wrong plan.
The material does not say whether the fewer volatile-function evaluations and single-row locking need user-facing documentation or a release note.
The material does not say how existing extensions using create_upper_paths_hook react to a NULL input relation.

prior_attempts.title: parallel distinct union and aggregate support patch
prior_attempts.who_objected: David Steele, David Rowley, Daniel Gustafsson
prior_attempts.quote: Many months on and this patch still needs a rebase to apply, and the thread has stalled. I'm marking this Returned with Feedback.
prior_attempts.reason: The entry was returned with feedback because the patch needed a rebase for many months and the thread stalled. It got no review for two commitfests, and David Steele and David Rowley said the author had not answered reviewers who suggested an unbuffered Parallel Partition style operator. The author posted a Redistribute version in September 2021, but the visible messages show no review of it.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 added new executor nodes (Parallel BatchSort, then Parallel Redistribute) that send tuples to workers. This series adds no executor node: each worker runs a local HashAggregate below Gather and the leader runs a final one. P2 stalled for lack of rebase and review, with no design objection recorded.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
prior_attempts.quote: The idea of making a cost-based choice of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound, but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't really have.
prior_attempts.reason:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P5 was reverted because a cost-based choice relied on multi-column distinct estimates that are not trustworthy. This series also picks a plan from a group estimate, but it checks the worst-case worker hash table against hash_mem when the estimate is weak.

objections.title: Implicit LIMIT 1 silently weakens row locking in existing UNION queries
objections.failure_scenario: An application runs `select status from (select status from jobs where status = 'pending' for update) s union select 'none'` to lock every pending job. After upgrade, patch 3 adds Limit 1 and only the first row is locked. Concurrent workers then take the same jobs, and the bug appears under load in production with no error or plan warning.
objections.argument: Message #1 says a locking clause in a non-pullable subquery or CTE "locks only the first row" and asks whether children with rowMarks should be excluded. So the point is open. The DISTINCT precedent covers new behaviour that users already accepted, but for UNION this changes what an existing query does after a major-version upgrade, without opt-in. Fewer volatile qual and CTE evaluations change visible side effects in the same way. The material names no release note or user-facing documentation for this change.
objections.author_must_show: Why not exclude children with rowMarks or volatile expressions from the implicit LIMIT 1, and what would users lose if they were excluded?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 confirms single-row locking and fewer volatile evaluations, and asks whether children with rowMarks should be excluded. DISTINCT's Limit 1 also changed existing queries on upgrade, so that contrast is weaker than stated, but the open question stands.

objections.title: HashAgg memory gate borrows the SetOp hash table estimator
objections.failure_scenario: A later release changes the SetOp hash table layout and updates EstimateSetOpHashTableSpace(). That edit also moves the gate on partial hash paths for DISTINCT and UNION. Existing DISTINCT queries change plan with no test or reviewer linking the two, and users see this as a regression after upgrade.
objections.argument: Patch 1 changes plan choice for existing SELECT DISTINCT queries, not only for the new UNION path, using EstimateSetOpHashTableSpace() as a "conservative allowance" for HashAgg. Message #1 supports this choice with one near-unique 200k-row case and calls a HashAgg estimator a follow-up. A committer would likely want the gate to use an estimator for the node that actually runs, so changes to one executor node cannot silently move planning for another.
objections.author_must_show: Why not size the gate with a HashAgg-specific estimate in this series, and what keeps future SetOp changes from shifting DISTINCT plans?

precedents.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".

critic.reasoning: Patch 1 changes plan choice for existing DISTINCT queries using a SetOp estimator, and message #1 supports this with one 200k-row case. P5 concerns unreliable statistics, so it does not support the point about coupling two executor nodes.

objections.title: No planning-time measurement for queries that do not benefit
objections.failure_scenario: An OLTP workload runs many short non-ALL UNION queries over small tables. Each query now builds extra partial paths and runs the constant check on every child. Total time rises from planning cost alone, and nobody sees this in EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution numbers.
objections.argument: All benchmarks in message #1 report execution time on 1M-row tables, from one laptop under WSL2 with 4 runs each. Patch 2 builds new paths whenever the input has partial paths, and patch 3 inspects every child of every non-ALL set operation. The proposal reports no planning-time numbers, so the cost for users who gain nothing is unknown.
objections.author_must_show: What is the planning-time overhead for short UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT queries with many children where neither optimization applies?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 reports only execution time. Small tables get no partial paths, so patch 2 adds little there, but patch 3 runs the constant check on every child of every non-ALL set operation and that cost is unmeasured.

refuted.title: New public upper stage and selfuncs API shaped for one plan shape
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension using create_upper_paths_hook handles UPPERREL_SETOP once per set operation. After upgrade it also gets UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP, possibly several times per query, with an output_rel that holds only partial paths. If it adds non-partial paths there, or caches per-query state, it builds wrong plans, and its users find out from bad results.
refuted.argument: Patch 2 adds an upper stage that the README calls UNION-only, guarded by an assertion and meant "in the future" for other set operations. Patch 1 adds estimate_num_groups_unreliable() and SELFLAG_USED_MULTIVAR_CLAMP. Once extensions code against these, the stage contract and the flag cannot change cheaply, even if INTERSECT/EXCEPT later need a different partial shape. The proposal does not say why the stage must be hook-visible now and cannot stay internal until a second user needs it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which extension or planned core feature needs UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP exposed through the hook now, and does the stage contract also fit INTERSECT/EXCEPT?

critic.reasoning: Postgres already passes its other partial upper stages to create_upper_paths_hook, and selfuncs already has SELFLAG_ flags, so the patch copies existing practice. An extension that switches on the stage ignores the new value, so the wrong-plan scenario needs code written for the new stage.

refuted.title: Second partial de-duplication path beside DISTINCT's existing one
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch fixes costing or memory checks in the partial DISTINCT path, for example in create_partial_distinct_paths(), and does not touch prepunion.c. UNION and DISTINCT then pick different plans for equivalent queries. Nothing fails loudly, so the gap shows up in later field reports of UNION being slower than DISTINCT over UNION ALL.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says DISTINCT already builds partial distinct paths, and that `select distinct * from (A union all B)` is the faster existing form. Patch 2 adds UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP and a setop-specific partial path next to UPPERREL_PARTIAL_DISTINCT. The author says create_final_distinct_paths() does not fit because UNION inputs have varno-0 Vars, no statistics and setop-specific MergeAppend. Patch 1 shares some helpers, but that answer does not show why UNION cannot be planned as DISTINCT over an appendrel. That approach would reuse the existing stage and hook contract, so it would add no second one.
refuted.author_must_show: Why can the planner not plan a non-ALL UNION as DISTINCT over its UNION ALL appendrel, reusing UPPERREL_PARTIAL_DISTINCT, so no new upper stage is needed?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 gives the reasons for not reusing the DISTINCT code: varno-0 Vars, no statistics, child-derived group counts and setop-specific MergeAppend. Postgres already plans UNION separately in prepunion.c, and patch 1 moves the shared path construction into common helpers.

refuted.title: Constant-child LIMIT 1 targets a query shape with no shown users
refuted.failure_scenario: An application runs a UNION whose non-pullable subquery branch uses FOR UPDATE and a constant target list. After upgrade, that branch locks only the first matching row, and the application's concurrency assumptions break silently. The user finds out through a race in production, not from an error.
refuted.argument: Message #1 shows the constant-branch case only on a synthetic benchmark, with no field report or user request. A branch like "select 100 from tb where id = 100" inside a UNION is unusual in real SQL. The cost is a behavior change in locking and volatile evaluation that reaches every user of such a query. The author cites the SELECT DISTINCT precedent, but DISTINCT users opted into that shape, while UNION users get the change without asking.
refuted.author_must_show: Which real applications or ORMs generate UNION branches with a single constant output row, and how often do such queries appear in field reports?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1: the failure scenario is the same locking change. The remaining demand point is weak because Postgres already applies this optimization to SELECT DISTINCT, and the other costs fall only on queries with a constant child.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Patch 2 adds UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP to create_upper_paths_hook; patch 1 adds estimate_num_groups_unreliable() and SELFLAG_USED_MULTIVAR_CLAMP.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: New partial HashAggregate paths for UNION, Limit 1 on constant set-operation children, and a new gate on existing partial DISTINCT hash paths.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Patch 3 can make a locking clause in a non-pullable subquery or CTE lock only the first row.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Implicit LIMIT 1 silently weakens row locking in existing UNION queries

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A new upper stage, a new test module, and a HashAgg memory gate tied to EstimateSetOpHashTableSpace().

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Patch 3 runs the constant check on every child of every non-ALL set operation at planning time.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Why not exclude set-operation children with rowMarks or volatile expressions from the implicit LIMIT 1, and what speedup would users lose?
Why does the hash_mem gate use EstimateSetOpHashTableSpace() and not a HashAgg-specific estimate in this series?
Which existing SELECT DISTINCT queries change plan because of the new gate in patch 1, and in which direction?
What is the planning-time overhead for short UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT queries with many children where neither optimization applies?
Does any existing create_upper_paths_hook user misbehave when called with UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP and a NULL input relation?

committability.owner_note: Needs a committer who knows upper-rel planning, set-operation planning in prepunion.c and group-count estimation in selfuncs.c. Nobody has replied in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for plan changes in existing DISTINCT and UNION queries, for the changed locking and volatile-evaluation behaviour, and for a hook stage that extensions may code against, across all future major versions.
committability.author_follow_up: No sign either way; the thread has one message, in which the author asks an open design question and names a possible follow-up estimator.

priority.reason: Plain UNION is common and message #1 reports about 2.6 times speedups for low-cardinality inputs, but only parallel plans and constant children gain. The series is about 140 KiB across planner.c, prepunion.c and selfuncs.c, and no committer has replied.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can confirm that the constant check matches the DISTINCT rules, that the hook contract with a NULL input relation matches existing stages, or how the gate changes existing DISTINCT plans.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: (ALTER SYSTEM) SET +=/-= operator support
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds `+=` and `-=` to SET and ALTER ... SET, so a GUC_LIST_INPUT setting such as search_path or shared_preload_libraries can have entries added or removed without knowing its current value. A second patch applies the same syntax to numeric settings, for example `ALTER SYSTEM SET max_worker_processes += 4`.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that the syntax works only in SQL, not in postgresql.conf, and that this could make a proper postgresql.conf version hard to add later. He also pointed out that ALTER SYSTEM writes an absolute value to postgresql.auto.conf, which then overrides later edits in postgresql.conf, and that one operator for both append and increment would limit future use. The author saw no workable postgresql.conf syntax and stopped work on the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: After pondering this in the back of my mind for a while, I think my gut feeling about this still is that it's not worth implementing something that doesn't work in postgresql.conf. The likelihood of ending up with something that makes it hard to to eventually implement proper postgresql.conf seems high.

precedents_retrieved.title: Partial aggregates push down
precedents_retrieved.summary: postgres_fdw pushes partial aggregation to the remote server for aggregates marked safe by a new pg_aggregate flag (set for min/max/sum/count). For aggregates with internal state, a new converter function runs locally and turns the remote aggregate result into the local partial-aggregate state.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra was still not convinced of the approach in the last review. He saw no clear path to aggregates with complex states such as avg(), and he doubted that the aggpartialpushdownsafe flag without version checks ensures the remote node represents the state the same way. The author agreed he did not know how to handle complex states, and postgres_fdw has no way to learn the remote server version at planning time. The visible messages do not show further discussion before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
1) It's not clear to me how could this get extended to aggregates with
more complex aggregate states, to support e.g. avg() and similar fairly
common aggregates.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rewrite undirected edge patterns in GRAPH_TABLE using UNION ALL
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the GRAPH_TABLE rewrite of undirected edge patterns (-[e]-) between the same vertex table from one OR join qual over both directions to a UNION ALL subquery on the edge table. The backward branch filters out self-loops so each edge appears once, and benchmarks showed large speedups over BitmapOr plans.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Ashutosh Bapat argued that the OR-to-UNION transformation belongs in the planner, where it would help all join-with-OR queries and could be cost based. An unconditional rewrite in the graph query rewriter would be useless once the planner does it, and misleading when statistics favour keeping the OR. The author agreed the work should move to the optimizer as a separate patch. SQL/PGQ was also reverted from master, leaving the patch nothing to apply against.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If OR transformation is implemented in the query optimizer, the
implementation in graph query is useless and, more seriously, misleading if
the correct statistics were to favour retaining OR.

precedents_retrieved.title: Partial aggregates push down
precedents_retrieved.summary: Let postgres_fdw push partial aggregation down to remote servers, so each shard computes a partial aggregate state and the local server finalizes it. Early versions handled simple aggregates such as count, min, max and sum, and later versions extended this to aggregates with internal states, using added partial aggregate functions and a remote version check.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas said two major areas of work remained before the feature could be committed. Approach #2, which does the pushdown with an SQL keyword instead of separate partial aggregate functions for each aggregate, still needed investigation. Sending serialized bytea states between servers that cannot fully trust each other also needed design work and consensus. The entry closed as returned with feedback because, as vignesh C wrote, there was "still some work" left.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: In addition, the problems around transmitting serialized bytea blobs between machines that can't be assumed to fully trust each other will need to be addressed in some way, which seems like it will require a good deal of design work, forming some kind of consensus, and then implementation work to follow.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent was rejected for a reason that still applies. P1, P2 and P3 stalled without a design objection. The P5 concern about unreliable group estimates is addressed in message #1 by the hash_mem gate, which follows the existing partial DISTINCT practice.

The new UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP hook call with a NULL input relation follows how the setop stage is already exposed, so I raise no compatibility objection there. Patches 1 and 2 add no syntax, GUC or dump-visible state.

The series changes only the planner. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog column, wire message or replication behavior, so pg_upgrade, standbys and subscribers are unaffected. The UPPERREL_PARTIAL_SETOP enum value and the new selfuncs symbols land in a new major version only, where extensions recompile anyway. Passing a NULL input relation to create_upper_paths_hook appears to follow how the existing UPPERREL_SETOP stage calls the hook, but this cannot be confirmed without the code. Fewer row locks in hidden locking clauses is a semantics question for another angle.

The proposal adds no privilege, role or exposure surface: workers run with the leader's privileges, RLS security quals still apply below the new Limit 1, and per-worker HashAgg memory stays bounded by hash_mem with spilling. Single-row locking in hidden FOR UPDATE subqueries is a concurrency semantics question for another angle.
Not applicable; the objections above are fixable design points. No committer has replied in the visible thread, so nobody has yet taken ownership of the planner changes.
The constant-child LIMIT 1 has no existing equivalent for set operations, so this angle raises nothing against patch 3.

Patch 2 (parallel partial de-duplication for UNION) targets a common construct and shows about 2.6 times speedups. A planner improvement for plain UNION needs no extra demand evidence, so I raise no demand objection against it.
